summary.text: The identity \((n-1)!a(n-1)=2^{n-2}\prod_{k=1}^{n-2}(2^k-1)\) and Fermat-based \(p\)-adic bounds show that, for any proper odd prime divisor \(p\mid n\), one has \(p\mid a(n-1)\), contradicting the hypothesis; if \(n=2^r\), Legendre’s binary digit-sum formula gives the analogous contradiction because \(n-1\) has at most \(r\) binary digits.  Thus \(n\) is prime, and if the order \(d\) of 2 modulo \(n\) were less than \(n-1\), then \(n\mid 2^d-1\) would force \(n\) to divide both the product and \((n-1)!\), impossible, so \(d=n-1=\varphi(n)\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 P_m:=\prod_{k=1}^{m-1}(2^k-1)\qquad(m\geq 1).
\]
Thus the sequence in the statement is
\[
 a(m)=\frac{2^{m-1}P_m}{m!}.
\]
We will first justify that this quotient is an integer and record the identity
\[
 m!a(m)=2^{m-1}P_m. \tag{1}
\]
We then exclude every possible composite value of \(n\), and finally prove the primitive-root assertion when \(n\) is prime.

Throughout, for a prime \(p\) and a positive integer \(x\), write \(v_p(x)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in \(x\). We use the following standard consequences of Legendre's formula. If \(x\geq1\), then
\[
 (p-1)v_p(x!)=x-s_p(x), \tag{2}
\]
where \(s_p(x)\) is the sum of the base-\(p\) digits of \(x\). Since \(s_p(x)\geq1\), this gives
\[
 (p-1)v_p(x!)<x,
\]
and hence
\[
 v_p(x!)\leq \left\lfloor\frac{x-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor. \tag{3}
\]
For \(p=2\), (2) says in particular
\[
 v_2(x!)=x-s_2(x). \tag{4}
\]
We will also use Fermat's theorem: if \(p\) is an odd prime, then
\[
 2^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p. \tag{5}
\]

First we prove a lower bound for the valuation of \(P_m\). For every odd prime \(p\) and every \(m\geq1\),
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor\leq v_p(P_m). \tag{6}
\]
Indeed, this follows by induction on \(m\). It is clear for \(m=1\), when \(P_1=1\). Passing from \(m\) to \(m+1\) adjoins the factor \(2^m-1\):
\[
 P_{m+1}=P_m(2^m-1).
\]
The integer
\(
\lfloor m/(p-1)\rfloor
\)
is equal to
\(
\lfloor(m-1)/(p-1)\rfloor
\)
unless \(p-1\mid m\), in which case it is larger by exactly one. In the latter case, write \(m=c(p-1)\). By (5),
\[
 2^m=(2^{p-1})^c\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
so \(p\mid 2^m-1\), and adjoining this factor increases the \(p\)-adic valuation by at least one. In the former case no increase is required. This proves (6).

We can now prove the integrality of \(a(m)\). Every factor \(2^k-1\) is odd, so
\[
 v_2(2^{m-1}P_m)=m-1.
\]
By (3) with \(p=2\), \(v_2(m!)\leq m-1\). If \(p\) is odd, then \(p\nmid2\), and therefore, using (3) and (6),
\[
 v_p(m!)
 \leq \left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor
 \leq v_p(P_m)
 =v_p(2^{m-1}P_m).
\]
Thus, for every prime \(p\), the valuation of \(m!\) does not exceed that of \(2^{m-1}P_m\). By unique prime factorization,
\[
 m!\mid 2^{m-1}P_m.
\]
Consequently \(a(m)\) is an integer and identity (1) holds. Notice also that \(a(m)>0\), since every factor in its numerator is positive.

We now establish two lemmas that will rule out composite \(n\).

First suppose that an odd prime \(p\) divides \(n\) and that \(p<n\). Write
\[
 n=pq.
\]
Then \(q\geq2\). We claim that
\[
 v_p((n-1)!)<v_p(P_{n-1}). \tag{7}
\]
To prove this, first observe the exact factorial valuation identity
\[
 v_p((pq-1)!)=v_p((q-1)!)+(q-1). \tag{8}
\]
Indeed,
\[
 pq-1=p(q-1)+(p-1).
\]
None of the \(p-1\) integers immediately following \(p(q-1)\) is divisible by \(p\), so
\[
 v_p((pq-1)!)=v_p((p(q-1))!).
\]
Among the factors \(1,2,\ldots,p(q-1)\), the multiples of \(p\) are \(p,2p,\ldots,(q-1)p\). Their contribution is one factor of \(p\) each, together with the \(p\)-adic valuations of \(1,2,\ldots,q-1\). Thus
\[
 v_p((p(q-1))!)=(q-1)+v_p((q-1)!),
\]
which proves (8).

Applying (3) to \((q-1)!\) gives
\[
 v_p((q-1)!)\leq
 \left\lfloor\frac{q-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor.
\]
Therefore (8) yields
\[
 v_p((pq-1)!)
 \leq \left\lfloor\frac{q-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor+q-1.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
 pq-2=(p-1)q+(q-2),
\]
so
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{pq-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor
 =q+\left\lfloor\frac{q-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor.
\]
It follows that
\[
 v_p((pq-1)!)<
 \left\lfloor\frac{pq-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor. \tag{9}
\]
Applying (6) with \(m=n-1=pq-1\), we have
\[
 \left\lfloor\frac{pq-2}{p-1}\right\rfloor
 \leq v_p(P_{n-1}).
\]
Together with (9), this proves (7).

Now use (1) with \(m=n-1\):
\[
 (n-1)!a(n-1)=2^{n-2}P_{n-1}. \tag{10}
\]
Because \(p\) is odd, \(v_p(2^{n-2})=0\). Taking \(p\)-adic valuations in (10), and using positivity of all factors, gives
\[
 v_p((n-1)!)+v_p(a(n-1))=v_p(P_{n-1}).
\]
By (7), the right-hand side is strictly greater than the first term on the left, so
\[
 v_p(a(n-1))\geq1.
\]
Thus
\[
 p\mid a(n-1). \tag{11}
\]

Suppose, contrary to the desired conclusion, that
\[
 n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}. \tag{12}
\]
Since \(p\mid n\), condition (12) implies
\[
 p\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}.
\]
Combining this with (11), we obtain \(p\mid2^{n-2}\). Since \(p\) is prime, this forces \(p\mid2\), impossible for an odd prime. We have proved:

If \(n>2\) has an odd prime divisor \(p<n\), then (12) cannot hold. \(\tag{13}\)

We next exclude powers of two. Suppose
\[
 n=2^r,
\]
where \(n>2\). Then \(r\geq2\). We have
\[
 r\leq 2^r-2=n-2; \tag{14}
\]
for example, this follows by induction from \(2^r\geq r+2\) for \(r\geq2\). Hence
\[
 2^r\mid 2^{n-2}. \tag{15}
\]
If (12) held, then (15) would imply
\[
 2^r\mid a(n-1),
\]
and therefore
\[
 v_2(a(n-1))\geq r. \tag{16}
\]

Again take valuations in (10). The product \(P_{n-1}\) is odd, so
\[
 v_2((n-1)!)+v_2(a(n-1))=n-2. \tag{17}
\]
By the binary form (4) of Legendre's formula,
\[
 v_2((n-1)!)=(n-1)-s_2(n-1).
\]
Here \(n-1=2^r-1\), whose binary expansion consists of exactly \(r\) ones. Thus
\[
 s_2(n-1)=r,
\]
and substituting into (17) gives
\[
 (n-1-r)+v_2(a(n-1))=n-2,
\]
so
\[
 v_2(a(n-1))=r-1.
\]
This contradicts (16). Therefore:

If \(n>2\) is a power of two, then (12) cannot hold. \(\tag{18}\)

We can now prove that any \(n>2\) satisfying (12) is prime. Every positive integer is either a power of two or has an odd prime divisor: remove all factors of two from its prime factorization; if anything remains, it has an odd prime factor. If \(n\) were composite and a power of two, (18) would contradict (12). Otherwise choose an odd prime \(p\mid n\). If \(p=n\), then \(n\) itself is prime, contrary to the assumption that it is composite. Hence \(p<n\), and (13) again contradicts (12). Thus \(n\) must be prime.

It remains to show that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo this prime \(n\). Since \(n>2\), it is an odd prime, so \(2\) is nonzero modulo \(n\). Let
\[
 d=\operatorname{ord}_n(2)
\]
be the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(n\). Fermat's theorem gives
\[
 2^{n-1}\equiv1\pmod n,
\]
so
\[
 d\mid n-1. \tag{19}
\]
By the definition of the order,
\[
 2^d\equiv1\pmod n,
\]
that is,
\[
 n\mid 2^d-1. \tag{20}
\]
We claim that \(d=n-1\). Suppose otherwise. Since \(d\geq1\), and since (19) implies \(d\leq n-1\), we would have
\[
 1\leq d<n-1.
\]
Thus the factor \(2^d-1\) occurs in
\[
 P_{n-1}=\prod_{k=1}^{n-2}(2^k-1).
\]
By (20), it follows that
\[
 n\mid P_{n-1}. \tag{21}
\]

Multiply the assumed divisibility (12) by \((n-1)!\). Using (10), we obtain
\[
 n\mid (n-1)!a(n-1)+(n-1)!2^{n-2}
   =2^{n-2}\bigl(P_{n-1}+(n-1)!\bigr). \tag{22}
\]
The prime \(n>2\) does not divide \(2^{n-2}\). Euclid's lemma applied to (22) therefore gives
\[
 n\mid P_{n-1}+(n-1)!. \tag{23}
\]
Together, (21) and (23) imply
\[
 n\mid(n-1)!.
\]
But none of the factors \(1,2,\ldots,n-1\) is divisible by the prime \(n\), so their product \((n-1)!\) is not divisible by \(n\). This contradiction proves
\[
 d=n-1.
\]
Finally, for a prime \(n\), Euler's totient is \(\varphi(n)=n-1\). Hence the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(n\) is \(\varphi(n)\), which is exactly the assertion that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\).

Therefore, for every integer \(n>2\),
\[
 n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}
\]
implies that \(n\) is prime and that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\), as required.
